parts.stem: Why did the peddler leave the public highway and enter the forest?

label: PYQ-style
stem: What was the peddler's theory about the world? Why did it give him pleasure? (40–50 words)
hint: Baits; trap closes; bitter revenge on an unkind world.
model_answer: The peddler believed the whole world was a huge rattrap. It tempted people with baits — riches, joys, food, shelter, warmth and clothes — and the moment anyone touched them, the trap closed. The idea pleased him because the world had been unkind to him; imagining others caught in its trap gave him a bitter satisfaction.

scheme.step: World as rattrap with baits listed; trap closes
Pleasure: revenge on an unkind world, imagining others trapped

label: PYQ-style
stem: Why did the peddler refuse the ironmaster's invitation but accept Edla's? (40–50 words)
hint: Fear of exposure vs compassion and freedom to leave.
model_answer: The ironmaster invited him as Captain von Stahle, and the peddler, carrying stolen money and knowing the mistake, feared exposure and the sheriff at a rich man's house. Edla, however, saw his fear and spoke with real compassion, assuring him he need stay only for Christmas Eve and could leave whenever he wished. Her kindness won him over.

scheme.step: Refused: false identity, stolen money, fear of sheriff
Accepted: Edla's compassion and promise of freedom to leave

label: PYQ-style
stem: Why did Edla insist that the peddler stay on even after his identity was discovered? (40–50 words)
hint: One day of peace; she had invited him; Christmas spirit.
model_answer: Edla felt responsible, since she had persuaded him to come. She also pitied a man who was chased from place to place all year, hungry and homeless, and wanted him to enjoy at least one day of peace and a proper Christmas. Her father's threat of the sheriff seemed to her against the spirit of the festival.

Wanted him to have one day of peace / Christmas spirit

label: PYQ-style
stem: 'The story is a testimony to the fact that human goodness, once awakened, can transform a person.' Trace the change in the peddler and show how Edla Willmansson brought it about. (120–150 words)
hint: Who he was → the theft → Edla's three acts (invitation, plea, gift) → the rattrap gift and letter → message.
model_answer:
The peddler begins as a bitter vagabond who sells rattraps, begs and steals, and who consoles himself with the thought that the world is a rattrap in which everyone is caught. He proves his own theory by robbing the crofter who had fed him, and feels trapped when he loses his way in the forest.

Edla Willmansson changes him. At the forge she notices his fear but speaks to him gently, promising that he may leave whenever he wishes. When his identity is exposed and her father wants the sheriff, she insists that he be allowed one day of peace and a Christmas like other people. She gives him her father's suit as a gift and invites him to return.

Treated for the first time with trust and respect, the peddler responds in kind. He leaves behind a rattrap containing the stolen notes to be returned to the crofter, with a letter signed Captain von Stahle — the dignity Edla gave him has become his own.

scheme.step: The peddler's earlier character and the theft
Edla's compassion: invitation, plea for one day of peace, gift and invitation to return
The change: money returned, letter, signature as captain
Message about goodness awakening goodness; expression and length

label: PYQ-style
stem: How does the metaphor of the rattrap work through the whole story, from the peddler's idle theory to his final letter? (120–150 words)
hint: Theory → baits → thirty kronor as bait → forest as trap → ironmaster's house as another possible trap → kindness as the way out → rattrap gift and 'raised to captain'.
model_answer:
The rattrap begins as a cynical joke. Making wire traps for a living, the peddler decides that the world itself is a rattrap, offering riches, food and shelter as bait and snapping shut on whoever touches them. The idea comforts a man the world has ill-treated.

The story then makes him live his metaphor. The crofter's thirty kronor are the bait; he grabs them and, lost in the forest, feels the trap close around him. At Ramsjö the invitation to a rich man's house, with a sheriff somewhere near, looks like another trap, and he refuses it in fear.

Edla's kindness turns the metaphor around. Trust and respect, not bait, draw him in, and they set him free. His parting gift to her is a rattrap — but this time it holds the stolen money being returned. His letter calls himself a rat who would have been caught had he not been raised to captain. The trap that catches people is greed; the key that opens it is compassion.

scheme.step: The theory and why it consoles him
Living the metaphor: money as bait, forest as trap, fear at Ramsjö
The reversal: kindness frees him; the rattrap gift and the letter
Conclusion on greed vs compassion; expression and length
